message.content:
The last common ancestor of a lion (family Felidae, order Carnivora) and a zebra (family Equidae, order Perissodactyla) is the most recent common ancestor of the two orders Carnivora and Perissodactyla.  
Both orders belong to the larger clade **Laurasiatheria** (the “Laurasian” mammals), so the common ancestor is the last common ancestor of Laurasiatheria.  

This ancestor lived roughly 70–80 million years ago, after the split between the major placental mammal groups (Laurasiatheria vs. Xenarthra). It was a small, probably insect‑eating mammal that gave rise to the diverse lineages that eventually led to modern cats and horses.
message.reasoning: The user asks: "What is the common ancestor of lion and zebra?" They want the common ancestor of lion and zebra. This is a biology question. We need to answer. There's no tool needed. Just answer. Probably the common ancestor is the last common ancestor of the family Felidae (lion) and Equidae (zebra). That would be a mammal from the order Carnivora vs Perissodactyla. The last common ancestor of all mammals? Actually lion is a cat, part of order Carnivora, suborder Feliformia. Zebra is an equid, order Perissodactyla. The last common ancestor of these two orders is the last common ancestor of all placental mammals, which is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria? Wait, lion is in Laurasiatheria (Crown group). Zebra is also in Laurasiatheria? Actually zebra is in Perissodactyla, which is also Laurasiatheria. So the last common ancestor of lion and zebra is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which is the last common ancestor of all living mammals except Xenarthra. But maybe we can say the last common ancestor of the families Felidae and Equidae is the last common ancestor of the superorders Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria. That ancestor lived about 70 million years ago. So answer: the last common ancestor of the clades Carnivora and Perissodactyla, which is the last common ancestor of the clade Laurasiatheria, which lived around 70 million years ago. Or we could mention the last common ancestor of the clade Euarchontoglires? No, that's wrong. So answer accordingly.
